narrative:
The 2026 Miami Marlins opened the season with a jolt of electricity, as newcomer Owen Caissie launched a two-run homer on Opening Day that set an optimistic tone for a franchise hungry to prove itself. Through April, the young roster flashed genuine upside — Graham Pauley delivered clutch doubles, Liam Hicks provided pop, and the bullpen showed flashes of competence. But the dark shadow of closer Pete Fairbanks loomed large almost immediately, as a pair of costly late-inning meltdowns in April erased leads that the offense had worked hard to build. The Marlins were a team capable of brilliance, yet perpetually undermined by their own relief corps.

The spring and early summer months told a story of tantalizing inconsistency. Javier Sanoja emerged as a quiet engine of the lineup, delivering timely doubles and proving himself a reliable table-setter, while Xavier Edwards and the supporting cast chipped in when it mattered. Yet every promising stretch seemed to collide with another Fairbanks implosion — a Shohei Ohtani ground-rule double, a Kyle Tucker walk-off single, a William Contreras three-run bomb — each one a gut punch that typified the Marlins' inability to hold late leads. Miami was not a bad team. They were, frustratingly, a just-good-enough team that kept finding new ways to let wins slip through their fingers.

As summer turned to August, the Marlins found themselves in a grinding battle for relevance in the Wild Card race. Heriberto Hernández and Joe Mack provided clutch moments, and a wild-pitch strikeout against Javier Sanoja in late August encapsulated the strange, chaotic energy that defined this roster. But the bullpen continued to hemorrhage games — Jarren Duran's grand slam off Cade Gibson in late August was a particularly savage blow — and the team's inability to shut doors when it mattered most slowly strangled their playoff hopes.

The final weeks of September offered moments of brilliance, including Sanoja's 30th double and Esteury Ruiz delivering in the clutch, but also crushing defeats like Jack Ralston surrendering a Corbin Carroll home run in a pivotal spot. When the dust settled at 80-82, the Marlins had scored nearly as many runs as they allowed, hit 168 home runs, and posted a respectable 4.09 ERA — a roster portrait of a team perpetually one reliable reliever away from contention. The 2026 season will be remembered as a testament to potential squandered and leads surrendered, a maddening exercise in almost that left Marlins fans wondering what might have been.

chapters.title: The Fairbanks Problem
chapters.description: Pete Fairbanks becomes the season's villain as a series of devastating bullpen collapses in April erase hard-earned leads and expose a critical roster flaw.

chapters.title: Sanoja Rises, Bullpen Burns
chapters.description: Javier Sanoja establishes himself as the team's heartbeat while Miami fights to stay relevant, but another round of late-inning disasters in July keeps them from gaining traction.

chapters.title: August at the Brink
chapters.description: The Marlins make a desperate late-summer push, mixing clutch hits with maddening collapses as their playoff window slowly closes.

chapters.title: September's Last Stand
chapters.description: Sanoja's 30th double and Ruiz's clutch hitting provide flashes of hope, but a series of crushing defeats seal Miami's fate outside the postseason.
